one_liner: Public-domain reference rANS coders in C/C++ headers; interleaved and SSE 4.1 decoders run 1.6-3.7x the scalar decode.
what_it_does: Three small header files implement range-variant asymmetric numeral systems (rANS) entropy coding: rans_byte.h (32-bit state, byte-wise output, works on any 32-bit target), rans64.h (63-bit state, emits 32-bit words, 64-bit targets only) and rans_word_sse41.h (16-bit word I/O with a 4-lane SSE 4.1 decoder). The API is a low-level arithmetic-coder style: you supply start/frequency per symbol, encode in reverse order into a buffer that fills from its end, and do symbol lookup yourself. Example programs (main.cpp, main64.cpp, main_simd.cpp, main_alias.cpp) build static order-0 models on book1 and show scalar, 2-way interleaved and SIMD use.
how_it_is_fast: rANS keeps the coder state in one integer, so several independent coders can share one byte stream with no signalling; interleaving 2 streams lets an out-of-order CPU overlap their dependency chains (the interleaving design is in Giesen's arXiv 1402.3392 paper). The encoders replace division with a precomputed fixed-point reciprocal (Alverson's integer division by reciprocals; 31-bit or 63-bit states so exact reciprocals fit). The SSE 4.1 decoder uses a fully unrolled slot table (freq/bias per slot, scale_bits 12) and branchless renormalization via a movemask-indexed pshufb shuffle table, so four lanes refill 16-bit words without branches. main_alias.cpp adds the alias method for O(1) symbol lookup with table size proportional to the alphabet.
when_to_use: You are writing your own compressor and want a small, readable, CC0 rANS core to copy and adapt rather than a full library
Static (per-block) order-0 or context-model probabilities where you can precompute encoder reciprocals and a decode slot table
Decode speed matters more than encode speed and you can split data into 2, 4 or 8 independent streams (interleaved or SIMD decode)
64-bit x86 targets where rans64 gives near-entropy precision with 32-bit word output
Learning or teaching rANS: the headers carry long comments explaining the math and the reciprocal trick
when_not_to_use: You need a drop-in compressor or a stable file format: the author states the code is 'not intended to be industrial strength' and only illustrates the idea
Peak throughput on modern AVX2/AVX-512 or NEON CPUs: the 16-way AVX2 version promised in the README never landed, and later siblings (hypersonic-rANS, htscodecs, rans_static) are several times faster
Non-x86 SIMD: rans_word_sse41.h requires SSE 4.1 and platform.h includes x86intrin.h; NEON support was requested in issue #6 and not added

Portable bitstreams across endianness with rans64 (README says its output is not endian-neutral), or 32-bit targets with rans64 (uses unsigned __int128 / __umulh; issue #8 reports '__int128 is not supported on this target')
Adaptive (per-symbol updated) models: rANS encodes in reverse, so adaptive coding needs buffering of symbols; an arithmetic or range coder is simpler there

integration.dependencies: none (rans_word_sse41.h needs <smmintrin.h> and the ALIGNSPEC macro from the example platform.h)
integration.min_toolchain: C99 for rans_byte.h and rans64.h (stdint.h); rans_word_sse41.h must be compiled as C++; rans64 needs GCC/Clang unsigned __int128 or MSVC __umulh; examples use MSVC or GCC on Windows or Linux
integration.platforms: rans_byte: any 32/64-bit; rans64: 64-bit targets only; rans_word_sse41: x86 with SSE 4.1
integration.thread_safety: Stateless inline functions over caller-owned state and buffers; safe across threads with separate state (not documented explicitly)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: the scalar and interleaved coders share the same API in rans_byte.h/rans64.h, but the SSE 4.1 decoder uses a different 16-bit-word stream format and needs a matching encoder layout

gotchas: Encode runs backwards: symbols last-to-first, output pointer starts at the buffer end and moves down; the SIMD renormalizer reads up to 8 bytes past the input end, so pad the buffer or finish with the scalar decoder

A single-symbol alphabet (freq equal to the full scale) expands output: issue #11 (open) shows 72 bytes of 'a' becoming 148 bytes with rans_word_sse41; reading RansWordEncPut, the renormalization bound overflows to 0 in that case so every symbol emits a 16-bit word. Special-case single-symbol blocks

The example drivers use a fixed 32 MB output buffer (out_max_size = 32<<20 in main.cpp); issue #10 reports 'bad decoder' and a free() crash on Silesia mozilla (~133 MB, ~39.8 MB compressed), which exceeds that buffer. Size buffers yourself
rans_word_sse41 is hard-wired to scale_bits 12 and an 8-bit alphabet; rans_byte asserts scale_bits <= 16 and frequency-1 symbols use a special reciprocal path
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick ryg_rans when you want the smallest, public-domain, well-commented rANS core to embed or study; for raw speed take hypersonic-rANS or htscodecs (AVX2/AVX-512 32-way rANS, several GB/s) or rans_static, and note that sserangecoding already reports beating ryg_rans' SSE decoder (577-619 vs 513-566 MiB/s).
verified_claims_summary: On book1 (order-0 static model, 14-bit probabilities for rans_byte) on a Sandy Bridge i7-2600K, the author's README shows decode at 22.0-23.5 clocks/symbol for scalar rans_byte, 13.7-14.2 for 2-way interleaved rans_byte, 10.6-11.2 for interleaved rans64 and 5.9-6.2 (520-551 MB/s) for the 8-way SSE 4.1 decoder, about 3.7x scalar rans_byte (derived from page data). The baseline is the author's own scalar rANS; compiler and flags are not stated and the author calls the setup 'not great' on a short file.
status_note: Finished reference code (last commit 2018-11-25, README dated Feb 2014) with two open issues and no maintainer replies since; CC0 public domain and only three headers, so trivial to vendor and adapt.
